tip: 'Être en vacances' = to be on vacation. Note the plural 'vacances' – always plural in French.
'Avoir mal à' + body part = to hurt: 'j'ai mal au ventre'. The article contracts: 'à' + 'le' = 'au'.
Time takes an empty 'il' in French, like weather does. 'Quelle heure est-il ?' is literally "what hour is it" – the 'il' stands for nothing, it just holds the verb.
French HAS your age, it doesn't say you ARE it. 'Quel âge as-tu ?' = "what age have you", and you answer 'j'ai 30 ans', "I have 30 years" – never 'je suis'.
'De l'' is 'some' before a vowel sound: 'de l'eau', 'de l'huile', 'de l'argent'. Same meaning as 'du' and 'de la'.
There's no one-word "home" here: 'il est à la maison' is literally "at the house". Heading home is 'rentrer à la maison'.
French normally uses "the" for body parts where English says "his": 'il a les cheveux noirs' is literally "the black hair", not "his black hair".
'Qu'est-ce que' = what, when asking about things or actions. Literally "what is it that".
In speech, 'on' almost always replaces 'nous': 'on mange' for 'we eat'. 'Nous' now sounds formal or written.
Weather 'makes' in French: 'il fait beau' is literally 'it makes nice' = it's nice out. Cold and hot too: 'il fait froid', 'il fait chaud'.
French can't drop the "some": 'je veux de la viande', never 'je veux viande'. That 'de la' is required even when English leaves it out and just says "meat".
'Avoir mal à' = to have pain in: 'j'ai mal au dos' (my back hurts), 'j'ai mal aux dents' (I have a toothache).
'Est-ce que' placed before a statement turns it into a yes/no question. It's the most common question form in spoken French.
Negation wraps the verb in two parts: 'ne manges pas'. In casual speech the 'ne' drops – you'll hear 'tu manges pas' – but writing keeps it.
'De quoi' = what...of/about. Use after verbs that take 'de': 'avoir besoin de', 'parler de', 'avoir envie de'.
After negation, 'du/de la/des' normally become 'de/d'': 'il y a du pain' → 'il n'y a pas de pain'.
In questions, 'est-ce que nous' sounds natural. The inverted form 'sommes-nous' is more formal.
English drops the article in 'any questions', but French keeps it: 'des questions'. 'Des' is the plural of 'un/une' and can't be skipped.
'Avoir hâte de' = to be eager to / can't wait to. Literally 'to have haste to'.
When inverting with 'il/elle/on', add '-t-' between vowels for sound: 'a-t-il un frère ?', 'va-t-elle ?'
'Lequel/laquelle' = which one. It agrees with the noun: 'lequel' (masculine), 'laquelle' (feminine), 'lesquels'/'lesquelles' (plural).
Drop the "a" before jobs: 'ma mère est professeure', not 'une professeure'. Same with 'il est médecin'.
'Avoir peur de' = to be afraid of. Another 'avoir' expression where English uses 'to be'.
'Avoir envie de' = to feel like / to want. 'J'ai envie d'un café' = I feel like having a coffee.
After a question word French can flip the verb and its noun: 'quand arrive le train ?' puts 'arrive' ahead of 'le train' – "when arrives the train".
After negation, 'des' becomes 'de', and 'd'' before a vowel: 'pas d'amis', not 'pas des amis'.
Before a vowel sound, 'vieux' becomes 'vieil': 'un vieil homme', never 'vieux homme'. It's purely to avoid two vowel sounds clashing.
'Devoir' means both "must" and "owe". 'Combien je vous dois ?' = "how much do I owe you" – here it's money owed, not obligation.
'Pouvoir' turns irregular when you invert it: 'puis-je', never 'peux-je'. 'En quoi puis-je vous aider ?' is the polite "how can I help you".
'Les magasins' – use 'les' for all/general plural nouns. 'Des' would mean 'some' stores.
